title: from ... to until since for
subtitle: from 1992 to 2001 / until Friday / since Monday / for three days
summary: Use from ... to and until for the start and the end of a time, since for a point in the past up to now, and for with a period of time.

lesson.heading: from ... to ...
lesson.text: We use **from ... to ...** to give the start and the end of a time. You can also say **from ... until ...**. Both are correct.

lesson.heading: until
lesson.text: **until** says when something stops. After **until** you can put a day, a month, a time, or a subject and a verb. **till** means the same as **until**.

examples.text: They're going away tomorrow. They'll be away **until Friday**.
I went to bed early, but I wasn't tired. I read a book **until 3 o'clock**.

lesson.note: *How long* takes **until**: '**How long** will you be away?' '**Until** Monday.' But *When* takes **on**: '**When** are you coming back?' '**On** Monday.'

lesson.heading: since + a time in the past
lesson.text: **since** goes from a time in the past to now. We use it with the present perfect (*have been*, *have done*).

examples.text: Joe is in hospital. He has been in hospital **since Monday**.
Sue and Dave have been married **since 1968**.
It has been raining **since I arrived**.

lesson.heading: What comes after until, since and for?
rows: Friday / December / 3 o'clock / I come back
three days / ten years / five minutes / a long time

lesson.heading: for + a period of time
lesson.text: We use **for** with a period of time: three days, ten years, five minutes, a long time. Do not use *since* here.

examples.text: Gary stayed with us **for three days**.
I'm going away **for a few weeks**.
Joe has been in hospital **for three days**.

lesson.heading: A finished time or a time up to now?

left.label: Finished: from ... to / until
left.text: The time is over. We use the past simple.

right.label: Up to now: since
right.text: The time started in the past and is still true. We use the present perfect.
examples: Now we live in Canada. We came to Canada **in** 2001.

lesson.text: **since** takes a point in time (*since Monday*) and **for** takes a period of time (*for three days*), not ~~since three days~~.

exercises.prompt: Alex came to England in 1999. Before that he lived in Canada. Alex lived in Canada ___ 1999.
exercises.explanation: until 1999 = that is when his time in Canada stopped.

exercises.prompt: Alex came to England in 1999 and he still lives there. Alex has lived in England ___ 1999.
exercises.explanation: since + a point in the past, with the present perfect: from 1999 to now.

exercises.prompt: We waited for Sue ___ half an hour, but she didn't come.
exercises.explanation: half an hour is a period of time, so we use for.

exercises.prompt: I was tired this morning. I stayed in bed ___ 10 o'clock.
exercises.explanation: until 10 o'clock = that is when the time in bed stopped.

exercises.prompt: 'How long did you stay at the party last night?' '___ midnight.'
exercises.explanation: How long ... ? takes until + the time it stopped.

exercises.prompt: Does each time expression go after since or after for?
'Have you just arrived?' 'No, I've been here ___ half past seven.'
exercises.explanation: half past seven is a point in time, and the sentence goes up to now.

exercises.prompt: Dan and I are good friends. We have known each other ___ ten years.
exercises.explanation: ten years is a period of time, so we use for.

exercises.statement: Joe has been in hospital since three days.
exercises.explanation: Joe has been in hospital for three days. Use for with a period of time.

exercises.prompt: Alex moved to England in 1999. Clare worked in a hotel from 1998 to 2001 and works in a restaurant now. Adam was a teacher from 1992 to 1998 and is a journalist now. Match each sentence with its ending.

pairs.left: Clare has worked in a restaurant

exercises.prompt: This is my house. I've lived here ___ I was seven years old.
exercises.explanation: since + a subject and verb: from that time in the past to now.

exercises.prompt: Somebody asks you 'Where have you been?' You waited twenty minutes. Put your answer in order.
exercises.answer: I've been waiting for you for twenty minutes.
exercises.explanation: twenty minutes is a period of time, so we use for.
